newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul stocks nosedive on North Korean tension.
newsitem.headline: Seoul stocks nosedive on North Korean tension.

text.p: South Korea's leading share index plunged Friday in the first sign that North Korean threats over a submarine incident were eating into business confidence.
Foreign investors are also starting to reassess their view of political risk in South Korea, analysts said.
The composite stock index shed 17.58 points, or 2.21 percent, to close at 776.43.

"This has left investors in horror," said Ahn Hyo-moon, a fund manager with Korea Investment Trust Co. Ltd., referring to Pyongyang's warning to retaliate over the deaths of 22 North Korean soldiers who landed by submarine two weeks ago.
Lim Seong-un of Daewoo Securities said the threat "has thrown cold water over the market."

South Korean Prime Minister Lee Soo-sung Friday warned of North Korean action against a group of isolated islands and ordered security tightened at airports and diplomatic missions against possible terrorist attack.
Sohn Young-bock of Samsung Securities said: "This incident has given a heavy blow to a market already hit by worsening economic fundamentals."
Concern over the slowing economy, weighed down by plunging prices for semiconductors, steel and oil products, has cast gloom over the market.

Blue chips were hit hard by the rising tension. Samsung Electronics shed 1,900 won ($2.30) to 64,400 ($78.10), steelmaker POSCO lost 100 won (12 cents) to 42,400 ($51.42) and electricity-monopoly KEPCO dropped 1,200 won ($1.45) to 26,500 ($32.14).
Financial shares were among the big losers, with the financial sub-index losing 18.28 points to 721.59.
"Some investors believe that one way or another there will be more infiltrations by North Korea. This was reflected in today's dive," Ahn said.
Even before the submarine crisis began, foreign investors were wary about Seoul shares despite the raising of the foreign stock ownership ceiling to 20 percent from 18 percent on Oct. 1.
"There have been rising inquries from foreign investors on country risk in Korea. They are expected to sit tight on the sidelines," Sohn said.
Analysts were divided in their views on how long political and military tension would unsettle the market.
